A Volatile Week Ends with Tech Stocks Down, Oil Up
 
Plus, Tesla’s Roadster launch gets a cool reception, and companies don’t like stock tokenization
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
Tesla’s Roadster. TESLA/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Tech stocks slid. An up-and-down week for tech ended with a thud Friday, with the Nasdaq composite off 2.1%. Worries about uncertain returns on big AI investments are bubbling up again, especially for the heavily-indebted AI cloud-computing company CoreWeave. CoreWeave fell 11.9% on the day, and is down more than 23% this week.

 

Treasury yields climbed. Yields have moderated overall this week as investors sought out safer assets, but they rose slightly on Friday. Helping push yields up was a Treasury department survey of bond dealers that didn’t signal a cut in the size of future longer-term debt auctions. That move that could have helped keep yields in check. Yields on the 10-year Treasury note rose to 5.1%—still below a recent high of about 5.3%.

 

Oil rose. Brent crude futures were up 3.7% and neared $110 a barrel, their highest levels since May. Higher oil prices also helped prop up Treasury yields, given their influence on inflation signals the Fed considers in its rate decisions.

 

Tesla fell. Investors weren’t impressed by Elon Musk’s flight-capable Tesla Roadster. Musk said the vehicle would debut in 2028. The company’s stock fell 2.1% on the day.

The outlook for data center power demand
 
As AI models scale, their massive computational needs are putting unprecedented pressure on power grids. Goldman Sachs Research projects AI will drive an increase of 170% in global data center power demand by 2030, adding the equivalent of Japan's entire electricity consumption.

One Big Story

 
 
SPENCER PLATT/GETTY IMAGES
 

A corporate rebellion against tokenizing stock trading has begun. Companies including AI chip maker Broadcom and telecom Verizon are objecting to the Securities and Exchange Commission’s move to tokenize their stocks. Turning their shares into tokens would enable round-the-clock trading, appealing to investors who have grown up on crypto. But some worry that it could create a shadow stock market, bending rules that try to ensure investors get the same prices no matter where they trade.
